item.title: Finding Steadiness When the Ground Feels Shaky
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear, well-structured English with useful vocabulary and concrete detail

Finding Steadiness When the Ground Feels Shaky

By Leo Babauta

These days, the world (and our lives) can feel out of control — alarming news, a wild political situation, global warming and economic markets all in turmoil.

When things feel this shaky and out of control, our emotions can spiral and it throws our lives into chaos. What can we do?

The practice I’m going to share with you today is how to find internal steadiness, when everything around you is unsteady.

The practice is to focus on attending to our internal state. To find calm and peace no matter what’s happening externally.

Let’s dive into it!

Focusing on What We Can Control

We can’t control the markets, what’s happening politically, how other people are acting, the ongoing climate change crisis, or the AI revolution. When things feel out of control, it can send us spinning.

So our practice will focus on what we can control: putting our attention on our internal state. We can’t necessarily control our inner state — if it’s in turmoil, we can’t always stop that — but just by resting our attention gently on the inner state, things can start to calm.

So let’s talk about how to practice.

How to Practice

First, just notice that you’re feeling shaky. Maybe you’re feeling a lot of uncertainty and overwhelm, maybe frustration or anger, maybe you’re feeling shaken up and in turmoil. Just notice it, and name it: what are you feeling?

Don’t get caught up in thoughts about what you’re feeling, or judgments. Just notice that it’s there, and name it. Don’t add a whole narrative, or catastrophize about it. It’s not a big deal to feel something.

Next, just rest your attention gently on the sensations of the feeling. That means notice how the feeling feels in your body, as physical sensations. Does it feel tight, does it move around? Just bring awareness to the physical sensation, and keep your awareness there — stay with it.

Breathe deeply and slowly, soothing your nervous system.

Let yourself settle down in the moment with whatever you’re feeling. It’s OK to feel turmoil — can you sit calmly in the center of the storm of what you’re feeling? This takes practice, so don’t expect to be any good at it at first. But you’ll start to get the hang of it, if you practice a few times a day for just a minute or two.

Slowly, you’ll develop the ability to sit calmly and openly in the middle of any storm.

And that’s when you’ll feel powerful: because you don’t need the world to change to find your inner calm. It’s always there, always accessible, and always beautiful.

item.title: The Human Habits That Still Matter
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail with useful vocabulary

The Human Habits That Still Matter

By Leo Babauta

These days, you can’t avoid hearing and thinking about AI — it’s all around us, and it’s taking over the world. So much of our lives are being automated … which in some ways is breathtaking.

In other ways, I think we can all feel that we’re losing something.

This is a moment to stop and reflect: what is important to remain human? What human skills do we want to protect?

Let’s explore some of those very human habits that we can’t let fall to the bots.

The Habits That Matter

While AI can generate a lot of amazing things, and help us in incredible ways … there are some things that are ours, as humans:

- Being present: The AI bots can’t actually be present with us. That’s for humans to do with each other. There’s something in our nervous system that gets soothed when we’re in the loving presence of someone we care about. There’s something that opens in us when we’re present with someone we’re learning about.

- Caring: One thing we notice from AI generated stuff is that it’s very intelligent … but there’s no feeling that it cares. Of course not — because AI doesn’t care. That’s for us humans to do, and it’s incredibly important in our lives. We can’t lose connection to what we care deeply about.

- Sitting with discomfort: I think technology is slowly seeping away our ability to be OK with discomfort. Our phones, computers, social media, AI, and the abundance of entertainment means that we can be comfortable all the time. But it’s a very human capacity to allow ourselves to sit in the middle of discomfort. And it matters: it’s how we expand, connect with each other, have difficult conversations where we disagree, and meet our resistance to doing hard things.

- Choosing what matters: Sometimes, we want things to be chosen for us, because we have so much decision fatigue. But AI can’t choose what matters, because nothing matters to it. That’s for us — we have to think deeply about what matters to us, and choose to step in that direction.

The Habit of Being Human

All of this is a choice: we can choose to care, to sit with discomfort, to be present with the world and each other, and decide for ourselves what matters.

And it’s a choice we can make a habit — something we do regularly, because we care about these human things. Because they matter to us.

I encourage us to make it a habit to do our focused work — the work that matters to us — in the presence of another human being. And have conversations with them, even if it’s uncomfortable. Go deeper, and discover something new together, without reaching for AI.

Notice when you reach for technology when you’re uncomfortable, bored, feeling resistance or uncertainty. And then turn towards that, as a human habit. Feel it. Only we can feel boredom, and sit with that discomfort. In this place, the deepest discoveries of humanity have been made. What would Aristotle, the Buddha, Epictetus, Shakespeare, Tolstoy, Jane Austen, Newton have created, if they had technology to keep them from being bored?

Choose to care about what you work on, what you put your attention on, who you spend your time with. Find a deeper appreciation for each of these, in each moment. Let yourself be filled with wonder, that great human experience that’s always available to us.

Slow down, and let yourself savor human connection and weirdness and huge loving hearts.

These are the human habits I urge you to care about. Automation will eat the tasks. But we are so much wilder than our tasks.

item.title: How to Stop Trying to Optimize Your Life
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail with useful vocabulary

How to Stop Trying to Optimize Your Life

By Leo Babauta

These days, so many people are trying to optimize their lives in every way — and I’m as guilty as anyone. Life optimization seems to be the theme for many of us.

But the thing is … it never ends. You can spend months trying to optimize every facet of your life … and you will still feel like more needs to be done. That’s because underneath the optimization mindset is the hidden message: My life as is at the moment isn’t good enough.

We want to optimize our health because our fear is that we’re not going to be able to handle the future without it. We want to optimize our productivity because we judge ourselves for not being more productive. We want to optimize our morning routines, sleep routines, finances, and more … because we fear that we’re not doing good enough at life.

This mindset stems from a fundamental dissatisfaction with our lives and ourselves.

We’re always looking toward a better future, instead of just living with gratitude in the life we already have in front of us.

This comes at a cost: we put pressure on ourselves, it stresses us out, we are comparing our lives to everyone else on social media, we’re rushing (because going slow isn’t optimal), we always feel behind, never done. Does any of that sound familiar?

So what can we do instead?

Let’s lay out some credos of the Unoptimized Life.

- Let some things be sub-optimal. It’s worth asking yourself why you want everything to be optimal — is there a fear that if it’s not the most optimal, you’ll be doing things wrong or failing? Entire industries have been formed on people wanting to optimize everything, and being afraid of missing out on what’s the absolute best. It’s OK to be inefficient or suboptimal, if it means hours of less stress. Have fun with a task, enjoy the activity, don’t worry about perfection. Wander and explore.

- Let yourself do things without an outcome in mind. What if you could start something and not need to get to a certain place. I’m learning the game of Go right now, and it’s fun to just learn for the sake of learning, without needing to “get good” or achieve a certain rank.

- Practice getting to “good enough.” Not everything needs to be absolutely perfect — in fact, most things don’t. You might explore getting to good enough … and then stopping there, and being satisfied with that.

- Don’t focus much on metrics. Sure, some things need to be tracked, but not everything does. Lots of meaningful things are better without being tracked or measured for progress.

- The big one: from improvement to appreciation. Instead of asking, “How can I make this even better?” … you might ask, “What’s already beautiful about this?” The practice of appreciation is deep and powerful.

Let yourself be human. You’re not an improvement project. You don’t have to always upgrade.

Growth is fun, but having a death grip on progress and perfection takes all the fun out of it. Let it be joyful! Let it come from curiosity and enjoyment, rather than all the ways we feel inadequate.

And practice just being here, without having to get anywhere.

item.title: The Phone Addiction Loop, & How to Break It
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail with useful vocabulary

The Phone Addiction Loop, & How to Break It

By Leo Babauta

I’ve talked to close to a dozen people recently who have been struggling with phone addiction — it seems to be widespread, across all generations these days.

It’s not just a trivial problem … it can cause sleep problems, have us fall behind on the things that are important to us, miss deadlines, get overwhelmed by how behind we are.

And maybe just as important: it’s not how many of us want to live our lives. We don’t want to be trapped in a phone addiction loop. We want to be doing things that feel meaningful and joyful.

Let’s talk about the phone addiction loop, and then how to apply the habit ideas I’ve learned over the years to break the loop.

How the Loop Works

It’s a fairly basic habit mechanism:

- You have a trigger (let’s say stress, overwhelm, boredom, feeling behind on things).

- You reach for the phone

- You get a quick reward.

And repeat. That’s the cycle, and it works that way for most addictive habits (food, alcohol, games, Youtube, social media, smoking, drugs).

So how do we change this?

First, Ask Why

Before you start to change something like this, ask yourself why you want to make the change. Is it just because you think you should, and you’re judging yourself?

If you’re coming from a place of “should,” you’ll just give up as soon as it gets hard.

If you’re doing it because you think there’s something wrong with you, and you’re hard on yourself … you’re only going to get discouraged and give up.

So instead, find a positive reason that’s meaningful to you. For example:

- I want to get good sleep and feel good during the day

- I have some creative work I want to get done

- I want to be more present with my loved ones

- I want to read more books

- I want to get more active and take good care of my body

What would be your meaningful reason? Write it down.

Then Create a Commitment & a Moat

Now make a commitment … not just to yourself but to others. Promise a close friend, your partner, an accountability group. Tell them your plan. Commit to accountability.

Then create a moat — something that makes it hard to get to the phone when the trigger happens. This will allow you to have awareness that your addiction loop has been triggered, and then allow you to do the next phase (below).

Some examples of moats:

- Put the phone in a different room, so you have to walk all the way across the house/office to get it. Leave it there, and only give yourself 2 minutes in the room with it.

- Give it to your spouse/friend/coworker and say, “Don’t give it back to me until (5pm, tomorrow morning, etc.).”

- Use a blocker app (or device like the Brick) but let someone else set the password so you don’t know it. Have it set to block you on a schedule.

- Lock it in a drawer/safe with a key, give it to someone else.

You might also make the phone less attractive: put it in greyscale mode, turn off notifications, and delete the most tempting apps.

The idea isn’t that you can never use your phone — it’s that the friction to use it is greatly increased, so that you are more intentional, and you know when the trigger is happening.

Deal with the Trigger

The secret sauce is not just to stop yourself from using it, but to find new ways of dealing with the trigger — usually boredom, anxiety/stress, overwhelm, or feeling bad about yourself.

If you’re feeling that, instead of using your phone to cope … what if you could find a healthier coping mechanism?

It’s important to bring awareness to when the trigger happens … when it does:

- Notice what you’re feeling when you want to reach for your phone. Bored? Feeling stressed, overwhelmed, anxious? Feeling bad about yourself or your life?

- Take a few breaths. Let your nervous system be soothed. If the feeling is intense, get up and move around, distract yourself with something else. You’re creating a tiny pause, where you have choice.

- Now try to choose an alternative to cope with the feeling, other than your phone.

What alternatives? You might experiment to see what works for you — throw a bunch of things at the wall and see what sticks!

Here are a few ideas:

- Deep breathing

- Go for a walk

- Do some exercise — pushups, yoga, etc.

- Talk to someone

- Make a gratitude journal — or just journal about your feelings

You might find your own ideas as well. You’re practicing being OK with a bit of discomfort, and finding a way to deal with it that feels healthy.

The Importance of Grace & Compassion

This isn’t going to be simple — like food, a phone isn’t something most of us can just quit. We have to find a balance in our lives, between being able to function, and overdoing it.

We’re interrupting the loop, instead of relying on willpower. We might even set some phone-free periods that will start to feel refreshing.

But we might slip up, and that’s OK. It’s a process, not a switch we just flip. We’re trying to break the loop rather than let it be a repeated cycle. Sometimes, we might not do so well, and in those cases, it’s important to give ourselves some grace. Be compassionate, not harsh.

You can do this!

item.title: When the Work Feels Hard
item.description:

When the Work Feels Hard

By Leo Babauta

Sometimes, it just feels like the work you’ve got in front of you is hard: you aren’t feeling up to it, you want to turn to distractions.

That’s completely normal — most of have these days. Or weeks, or even months, when things just feel hard. It’s important not to be too tough on ourselves, and give ourselves grace for not being super fired up and productive all the time. We’re human.

That said, how do we deal with this feeling that the work is hard? There isn’t a simple answer, so I’m going to share a handful of ideas with you today.

1: Take a temperature check

As humans, we have so many things that might affect whether we feel motivated or not. It’s good to do a bit of a reflection, and see what might be contributing. That’ll help you sort it out.

Some things to check on:

- How’s your sleep been lately?

- Are you feeling high stress from your life, or high anxiety in general? Is your life outside of work super busy or chaotic?

- Have you been moving your body, in ways that make you feel generally healthy? Do you have health issues affecting you?

- Has something happened that got you feeling low? Is it possible you’re suffering from mild (or worse) depression?

- Is there something about the work you’re doing that’s scary, or that gives you a lot of resistance or overwhelm, that you’re trying to avoid? Are there unknowns that are making it feel tough?

- Anything distracting you that you’re obsessed with? Anything weighing on you heavily? Any grief or anger?

You might have more than one of these be true, or maybe it’s something else. The key idea is to take a brief assessment — be honest with yourself.

Once you have an idea of what might be making things hard, it can help to start to address them. If you have depression, get some mental health support. If you are having some emotional issues, talk to somebody, or do some journaling, to process the emotions. If there’s fear or overwhelm, can you make it smaller so it’s less scary and overwhelming?

There might not be easy answers, but at least taking a look at the issues and starting to address them is the way to go. Small steps. The idea of “work is too hard” is the symptom, not the problem.

2: Let yourself play

If work is feeling too hard … then let yourself play. Take a break from the hard things and then go have some fun doing something else! It might be work, or it might be getting outside and exploring, without a phone. Or reading something fun.

Then, after a bit of a break (for an hour, or a day, or more if needed and possible) … come back to the work but bring a lighter sense of play.

There isn’t a right way to bring play to your work … play with it! Be lighthearted, and have fun.

3: Stay in relationship with the work

Just because the work is hard, doesn’t mean you have to just walk away from it. You might not be able to completely go full in with it … but you can stay connected to the work.

Stay in relationship with the work — meaning don’t just drop off.

That might mean just doing a little work for the next few days, whatever you can manage. It might mean letting people know you can’t get things done when they’re expecting it, and renegotiating deadlines or other dates.

It could also mean taking a part of your work that feels meaningful — just a chunk of it — and going somewhere else to work on it. Go to a coffee shop, or a park, or a library. Play some relaxing music (in your earbuds, if you’re in public!).

Or let yourself go for a long walk, and just reflect on things. It’s a way to go deeper without doing the part that feels too hard.

4: Work your way back

If you do fall away from the work a bit, it can be hard to come back to it. That’s OK, it’s just a bit like going uphill instead of walking on normal ground. Sometimes we have to go uphill, right?

The idea is to find a way to ease yourself back into it. It’s harder coming back, so take small steps. Don’t expect yourself to be running right away.

When I come back after falling off, I give myself gentle days, and just do some of the easy stuff. Small batches, with breaks. Make it lighthearted.

What would be an easy way to bring yourself back?

Source: Zen Habits | Published: 2026-09-04 00:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The Mental Habits We Practice the Most
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail with useful vocabulary

The Mental Habits We Practice the Most

By Leo Babauta

There’s an old idea, often misattributed to Aristotle, that “we are what we repeatedly do.” That idea is true of our physical acts, but also of our mental habits.

What we’re practicing the most is what we think every day, and that becomes who we are.

For example, if we’re constantly complaining (even just in our own minds), that’s what we’re practicing all the time … and that shapes our experience of life, and how we impact other people.

The mental habits we’re practicing all day long are incredibly important in our lives — and yet we’re often not even aware we’re doing them.

Some of the most common mental habits that can have negative impacts on our lives:

- Complaint

- Blaming others

- Telling ourselves it’s OK to put something important off for one more day

- Deciding we need to check email, messages, social media one more time before focusing on the things that matter

- Self-criticism

- Judging other people

- Worrying about what everyone else thinks

- Ruminating on past mistakes or past hurts

- Limiting ourselves by how we see ourselves (I’m not smart enough to do that)

- Worrying about the future or possible failure

- Stressing ourselves out with all the things we think we need to do

- Getting stuck in indecision because it’s overwhelming or hard to choose the “right” decision

Do any of these feel familiar? They all have a big impact on our lives if we’re practicing them over and over, every day.

Let’s talk about how to shift these patterns by practicing new ones.

Practicing Different Mental Habits

The idea is to come up with replacement habits, and to practice them every day, as often as you can.

Start by noticing which negative mental patterns you practice regularly — do you notice any of the ones above?

Try to spot them as they happen: if you’re complaining, can you notice when you’re in the act of complaining?

Then practice the replacement mental habit. If you do this, you’ll start to replace the old habit with the new one, and it will start to become your default over time. It takes concerted effort, but the payoff is huge.

Some ideas for replacement mental habits:

- Gratitude and appreciation instead of complaint

- Taking responsibility for your part, instead of blaming others

- Putting important things as a priority that you’re committed to, instead of putting it off for one more day

- Focusing on the things that matter first, before allowing yourself to check email, messages, social media

- Self-appreciation, instead of self-criticism

- Appreciating the great quality of other people, instead of judging them

- Caring about what you think, instead of worrying about what everyone else thinks

- Acceptance, instead of ruminating on past mistakes or past hurts

- Expanding our view of ourselves, instead of limiting ourselves by how we see ourselves

- Focusing on what we can control, instead of worrying about the future or possible failure

- Focusing on one thing right now, instead of stressing ourselves out with all the things we think we need to do

- Making a choice from the gut, instead of getting stuck in indecision because it’s overwhelming or hard to choose the “right” decision

You might have other ideas for replacements — that’s OK, these are just ideas. Decide for yourself what would be most helpful.

In the end, it’s about deciding what we want to practice every day — the things that will lead to the lives we want, or that will keep us stuck.

Source: Zen Habits | Published: 2026-08-28 00:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The September Health & Fitness Challenge
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

The September Health & Fitness Challenge

One of the hardest things to do as we create a better life is to show up for yourself regularly.

But we can train that. And one of my favorite ways to do that is with a health & fitness challenge — where you commit to showing up for your body and yourself every day. And prove to yourself that you (and your health) matter.

In September, I’m launching a 6-week Health & Fitness Challenge for my Fearless Living Academy members … and I’d love for you to join us!

Here’s how the challenge works:

- Sign up for Fearless Living Academy and then join the challenge in our Circle space (our community forum).

- Commit yourself to something every day for 6 weeks. You choose: some fitness challenge (yoga every day, running and weightlifting alternately every day, eating 5 vegetables a day, etc.).

- You get a video each week from me, meant to help you practice showing up for your commitment.

- Hold yourself accountable each week, and share how it’s going with the challenge group.

- Learn, grow, get stronger, and build the muscle of showing up!

It’ll be fun!

What You’ll Walk Away With

Here’s what we’re aiming for you to get out of this:

- You’ll learn about what it’s like to show up for your body, and learn what gets in the way (and how to handle that).

- You’ll create a non-negotiable habit that you chose and tested over the course of 6 weeks.

- You’ll start to recognize your patterns, and your own sabotage triggers (travel, stress, low motivation days), because you’ll have hit them during the challenge and practiced navigating them.

- You’ll learn a repeatable framework for creating any kind of practice for yourself going forward.

This challenge, then, becomes proof-of-concept for how you build solid habits in general.

This isn’t a fitness challenge that focuses on streaks or perfection, nor one that is focused on a specific outcome (lose weight, etc.).

This is processed-focused, and it’s a practice of fearlessness — show up for yourself even when it’s challenging.

Six Weekly Themes

Our structure is to have a new theme for each of the 6 weeks:

- Commit & Start: Pick your daily action, and make it small and doable. Declare it publicly, and get started!

- Show Up with Curiosity: Start to explore the habit, and bring curiosity — see what you can discover and appreciate about the habit process.

- Find Your Resistance: Identify exactly when/why you want to skip it (mornings? travel? mood?) — get curious, not critical.

- Build Your System: Design your environment. Remove friction, set up new reminders, find workarounds for your obstacles.

- Push Through the Middle: The motivation dip often happens by week 5 … this week is about identity (“I’m someone who does this”) over motivation.

- Reflect: Reflect on the 6 weeks, decide what stays post-challenge, celebrate the proof of what you care about.

It’ll take 6 weeks to build this deeper self-trust that you’ll show up for yourself Not perfectly. And it won’t be easy. But you’ll practice curiosity, courage, and a willingness to learn in the midst of the challenge.

Are you ready to join us? Join Fearless Living Academy for the September Health & Fitness Challenge, and let’s start.

item.title: One Tab, One Task, One Breath
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail with useful vocabulary

One Tab, One Task, One Breath

By Leo Babauta

Let’s do a quick test: how many tabs do you have open right now? How many apps on your phone or computer? How many tasks are competing for your attention right now?

Let’s also be honest about something: most of us are working in a constant state of fragmentation — so much so that it feels completely normal, and don’t even notice the effects it has on us.

I blame the environment rather than the individual person — but that said, I think there are things we can do to change our environment and reclaim our focus and our sanity.

The Fragmentation Problem

Our work environments have us constantly surrounded by things trying to claim our attention. This creates busyness and fragmented attention, and sacrifices depth and focus.

Every email, every message, every open tab is another claim on our attention. It drains our cognitive bandwidth.

As a result, we’re always half-present. Half in, no matter what we’re doing.

And again, it’s not a failure of you as a person — it’s just the environment that has been created all around you.

The Three-Part Practice

We can reclaim that bandwidth and focus with a three-part practice …

One Tab: Close every tab and app that isn’t the work you have to do right now. You might have a million tabs open — save them or close them. You don’t need them all right now. Close any open apps that you don’t need. Put your phone in silent mode and put it somewhere else as well. Clear everything so you can reclaim your attention.

One Task: Before you sit down to do something, name the one thing you’re going to actually focus on. You might need to open your task list and take a look, but choose something. Commit to focusing on it. It can also help to set a timer, for 10 or 20 or 30 minutes, to remind you that you’re focusing on one task right now.

One Breath: Before you begin on your one task, take a slow, deep, conscious breath. Be fully present with the breath, and let it release any tension you have. Let it be a prayer to start your task with focus and intention.

This breath signals that you’re present for this one task. Everything else is put on hold — in fact, there’s nothing else in the universe but this one thing.

This is a simple, powerful ritual to signal your conscious intention and to practice the focus that you’d like to have in your life.

The Practice Needs to Be Simple

With everything demanding our attention, we need to simplify in order to reshape our focus.

That’s why this practice is so simple. We narrow everything down to one tab, one task, one breath. And in doing so, we are retraining our brains to simplify.

This is radical simplicity — not necessarily doing less, but being fully present with what we choose to do.
